subject: biology
title: Digestion and absorption
key_idea: Digestion uses hydrolysis to break large molecules into small ones that can cross cell membranes. The products are absorbed in the ileum, by co-transport for amino acids and monosaccharides, and by micelles for lipids.

blocks.text: Large biological molecules are too big to cross cell membranes. Digestion hydrolyses them into smaller molecules that can be absorbed.

items.meaning: A reaction in which a bond is broken by adding water.
An enzyme that hydrolyses the glycosidic bonds in starch to give maltose.
An enzyme in the cell-surface membrane of ileum epithelial cells that hydrolyses a disaccharide into monosaccharides.

items.text: Salivary amylase, and then pancreatic amylase in the small intestine, hydrolyse starch to maltose.
Maltase, bound to the membrane of epithelial cells, hydrolyses maltose to two glucose molecules.
Sucrase hydrolyses sucrose to glucose and fructose. Lactase hydrolyses lactose to glucose and galactose.

items: Digestion is hydrolysis.
Amylase makes maltose from starch.
Membrane-bound disaccharidases produce monosaccharides at the surface of the epithelial cell.

blocks.text: Lipids are insoluble in water, so they need bile salts as well as an enzyme.

items: **Lipase** is made in the pancreas. It hydrolyses the ester bonds in triglycerides to give monoglycerides and fatty acids.
**Bile salts** are made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. They emulsify lipids.
Emulsification breaks large droplets into many smaller ones. This greatly increases the surface area, so lipase can act faster.
Lipase hydrolyses triglycerides to monoglycerides and fatty acids.
Bile salts emulsify lipids and increase the surface area for lipase.

blocks.text: Three types of peptidase work together to hydrolyse peptide bonds.

parts.name: Amylase
parts.detail: Hydrolyses starch to maltose. Made in the salivary glands and the pancreas.

parts.name: Membrane-bound disaccharidases
parts.detail: Hydrolyse disaccharides, such as maltose, sucrose and lactose, to monosaccharides. Found on the epithelial cell membrane.

parts.name: Lipase
parts.detail: Hydrolyses triglycerides to monoglycerides and fatty acids. Made in the pancreas.

parts.name: Endopeptidases
parts.detail: Hydrolyse peptide bonds within a polypeptide, which makes shorter chains and creates more ends.

parts.name: Exopeptidases
parts.detail: Hydrolyse peptide bonds at the ends of a polypeptide, removing single amino acids.

parts.name: Membrane-bound dipeptidases
parts.detail: Hydrolyse a dipeptide into two amino acids. Found on the epithelial cell membrane.

items: **Endopeptidases** hydrolyse peptide bonds inside the polypeptide chain. They break it into shorter chains.
**Exopeptidases** hydrolyse peptide bonds at the ends of the chains, removing one amino acid at a time.
**Membrane-bound dipeptidases** hydrolyse dipeptides into amino acids at the surface of the epithelial cell.
Endopeptidases increase the number of ends, so exopeptidases have more places to act.
Endopeptidases cut inside the chain and exopeptidases cut at the ends.
Dipeptidases finish the job at the epithelial cell surface.

blocks.text: The cells lining the ileum absorb the products of digestion. The mechanism depends on the molecule.

rows: Co-transport with sodium ions, by a carrier protein. Glucose then leaves the cell by facilitated diffusion.
Co-transport with sodium ions, by carrier proteins.
Carried in micelles, then diffuse across the membrane.

items: Sodium ions are actively transported out of the epithelial cell into the blood. This lowers the sodium concentration in the cell.
Sodium ions then diffuse into the cell from the gut, down their gradient, through a co-transporter protein.
Glucose or an amino acid is carried into the cell on the same protein, even if it must move against its own gradient.
The solute then diffuses into the blood, which keeps the concentration in the cell lower than in the gut.
Bile salts surround monoglycerides and fatty acids and form tiny droplets called micelles.
Micelles carry the products to the membrane of the epithelial cell, and release them.
Monoglycerides and fatty acids are lipid-soluble, so they diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer.
Micelles keep a high concentration of lipid products next to the membrane, which maintains the gradient.
Sugars and amino acids are absorbed by co-transport with sodium ions.
Lipid products are carried by micelles and diffuse across the membrane.

checks.q: Explain the roles of endopeptidases and exopeptidases in the digestion of proteins.
checks.a: Endopeptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds within the polypeptide, producing shorter chains and more ends. Exopeptidases hydrolyse bonds at the ends of the chains, removing single amino acids.

checks.q: Describe the role of bile salts in the digestion and absorption of lipids.
checks.a: They emulsify lipids into smaller droplets, which increases the surface area for lipase. They also form micelles with monoglycerides and fatty acids, which carry them to the epithelial cell membrane.

checks.q: Explain why glucose can be absorbed from the ileum when its concentration in the gut is lower than in the cell.
checks.a: Glucose is absorbed by co-transport with sodium ions. Sodium ions diffuse in down their gradient through a carrier protein, which carries glucose in with them. The sodium gradient is maintained by active transport of sodium out of the cell.
